summary: MPL provides IPv6 multicast forwarding in low-power, lossy networks without building or maintaining any multicast tree. Messages are disseminated to all forwarders in an MPL domain using the Trickle algorithm. This standards-track RFC defines the protocol and its two operating modes, one that is proactive and one that is reactive.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast is sending one message to many recipients. The usual way to do it is to build a tree of routers that forwards the message along the branches, and every router on that tree has to keep the tree up to date. This RFC describes a different approach for networks of small, battery-powered devices: no tree at all, just repeated sending with a small amount of bookkeeping at each device.

questions: multicast for low power lossy networks
multicast protocol for low power lossy networks
how does mpl use the trickle algorithm
subtitle: Multicast forwarding for constrained networks, with no routing tree to build or maintain.

tldr.problem: Multicast normally needs a forwarding tree that every router maintains, and in a low-power and lossy network the cost of building and keeping that tree can be prohibitive. Memory limits mean devices may hold only a few routes, and in wireless networks the topology information needed grows quickly with the number of nodes.
tldr.mechanism: MPL disseminates a multicast message by flooding it, with no tree at all. Each forwarder keeps a small per-seed record of the sequence numbers it has seen, and uses the Trickle algorithm to time retransmissions. Two modes are provided: proactive forwarding, which retransmits on a timer, and reactive forwarding, where neighbours exchange small control messages that reveal who is still missing a message.
tldr.outcome: Every MPL forwarder in a domain receives the message, and each device that starts a dissemination keeps only small, constant state. The cost is that the same message is sent several times, and the RFC notes that if attackers can reach the network, MPL should not be used there.

today: RFC 7731 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2016, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is designed to work with the routing protocol for low-power networks in RFC 6550, and it uses the Trickle algorithm from RFC 6206.

sections.title: Why Multicast Is Hard in Constrained Networks
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks operate under strict constraints on communication, computation, memory and energy, and those constraints may rule out the existing IPv6 multicast routing and forwarding mechanisms. Traditional IP multicast delivery relies on topology maintenance to discover and keep routes to all subscribers of a multicast group, and maintaining such topologies in these networks is costly and may not be feasible with the resources available.

Memory constraints may limit devices to maintaining links or routes to one or a few neighbours. For that reason the Routing Protocol for Low-Power and Lossy Networks specifies both storing and non-storing modes, and the non-storing mode lets routers keep only one or a few default routes towards a border router and use source routing to forward messages away from it. For the same reasons an LLN device may not be able to maintain a multicast routing topology at all.

The dynamic properties of wireless networks make the cost of maintaining a multicast routing topology prohibitively expensive. Topology maintenance in a wireless environment may involve selecting a connected dominating set to forward multicast messages to all nodes in an administrative domain, and existing mechanisms often require two-hop topology information, whose cost grows polynomially with network density.

MPL provides IPv6 multicast forwarding in constrained networks. It avoids constructing or maintaining any multicast routing topology, disseminating messages to all MPL forwarders in an MPL Domain, and by using the Trickle algorithm it needs only small, constant state for each device that starts a dissemination. The Trickle algorithm also makes MPL density aware, so the communication rate scales logarithmically with density.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary multicast depends on every router knowing the shape of the network, and that is expensive on small battery-powered devices. MPL replaces the tree with repeated sending: each device keeps only a short record of what it has already passed on, and there is no shared picture of the network to maintain.

sections.title: How MPL Disseminates a Message
sections.content:
The goal of MPL is to deliver multicast messages to all interfaces within an MPL Domain that subscribe to the message's destination address. It does so with a controlled flood.

When it has a multicast message to forward into a domain, the MPL Seed generates an MPL Data Message that carries the MPL Domain Address as the IPv6 destination address, the MPL Seed Identifier, a newly generated sequence number and the multicast message itself. If the multicast destination address is not the MPL Domain Address, IP-in-IP tunnelling is used to encapsulate the message inside the MPL Data Message, which preserves the original IPv6 destination address.

On receiving an MPL Data Message, a forwarder extracts the seed and sequence number and decides whether the message has been seen before, using the domain's Seed Set and Buffered Message Set. If the sequence number is below the lower bound kept in the Seed Set, or a message with that sequence number is already in the Buffered Message Set, the message is old. Otherwise it is new. For each new message the forwarder updates the Seed Set, adds the message to the Buffered Message Set, processes its payload, and multicasts the message a number of times on all interfaces participating in the same domain.

Two forwarding strategies are available. With proactive forwarding, a forwarder schedules retransmissions with the Trickle algorithm without any prior sign that neighbours have not received the message, and after transmitting a limited number of times it may stop. With reactive forwarding, a forwarder multicasts link-local MPL Control Messages using Trickle, and uses them to discover new data messages that neighbours have not received; when it learns that a neighbour is missing one, it schedules that message for transmission. The two strategies are not mutually exclusive and may be used at the same time in the same domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The device that starts the dissemination wraps the message with a seed identifier and a sequence number, and sends it to the domain's multicast address. Every forwarder that receives it checks the number against what it has already seen, and if it is new, passes it on and remembers it. The sequence number is what makes the repeated sends recognisable as repeats.

sections.title: The Information Base
sections.content:
A node records the protocol state it needs in four sets. The Local Interface Set records the local MPL interfaces and the unicast addresses assigned to them. The Domain Set records the MPL Domain Addresses and the local interfaces that subscribe to those addresses. Each MPL Domain has a Seed Set, which records information about messages received from an MPL Seed, and each domain has a Buffered Message Set, which records recently received messages from a seed.

A Seed Set entry is a tuple of the seed identifier, a minimum sequence number and a lifetime. The minimum sequence number is the lower bound representing the oldest message the forwarder is willing to receive or transmit, and any message with a lower sequence value MUST be ignored. An MPL Forwarder MUST NOT free a Seed Set entry before the remaining lifetime expires.

A Buffered Message Set entry is a tuple of the seed identifier, the sequence number and the data message itself. All messages in the set MUST have a sequence number greater than or equal to the minimum sequence number for that seed, and when the minimum is raised the forwarder MUST delete the messages that fall below it. When memory is limited, a forwarder SHOULD reclaim memory by raising minimum sequence numbers and deleting the corresponding buffered messages, and by deleting expired Seed Set entries along with their buffered messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Each device keeps four short lists: its own interfaces, the domains it takes part in, one entry per source of multicast traffic, and the messages it is currently passing on. The per-source entry holds the lowest sequence number the device still cares about, and the buffered list holds the messages themselves so that they can be sent again.

sections.title: The MPL Option and the MPL Control Message
sections.content:
The MPL Option is carried in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options header immediately following the IPv6 header of an MPL Data Message. Its Option Type is 0x6D. The S field is a 2-bit value that gives the length of the seed identifier: 0 means the seed identifier is the IPv6 source address and is not carried in the option, 1 means a 16-bit unsigned integer, 2 means a 64-bit one and 3 means a 128-bit one. The M flag, when set to 1, says that the sequence value is known to be the largest sequence number received from that seed. The V flag says whether the option conforms to this specification, and messages with V set to 1 MUST be dropped. The rsv field is reserved, MUST be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception. The sequence field is an 8-bit unsigned integer that orders the messages from a given seed, and the seed identifier names the seed that started the dissemination. Nodes that do not understand the MPL Option MUST discard the data message, which is why the three high-order bits of the Option Type are set to 011.

The MPL Control Message is an ICMPv6 message with Type 159 and Code 0, sent to the link-scoped MPL Domain Address with a Hop Limit of 255. It carries a list of MPL Seed Info entries, one for each entry in the domain's Seed Set. Each entry holds the minimum sequence number for that seed, a 6-bit length of the buffered-messages field, the seed identifier, and a bit vector in which the i-th bit represents the sequence number min-seqno plus i, with 0 meaning the message is not buffered and 1 meaning it is. The entry has no octet alignment requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Two messages carry the protocol. The data message is the multicast traffic with an extra header field holding the source identifier and the sequence number. The control message is a small neighbour-to-neighbour report listing, for each source, which sequence numbers the sender already has and which it is still willing to accept.

sections.title: Processing Data and Control Messages
sections.content:
On receiving an MPL Data Message, the forwarder first processes the MPL Option and updates the Trickle timer associated with the message if one exists. It MUST then either accept the message and enter it in the Buffered Message Set, accept it and raise the minimum sequence number in the Seed Set to one greater than the message's sequence number, or discard it without changing anything. If a Seed Set entry exists for the seed, the message MUST be discarded when its sequence number is below the minimum or when a message with that number is already buffered. If no entry exists for the seed, a new one MUST be created before the message is accepted.

If the message is accepted, the lifetime of the Seed Set entry is reset, and if PROACTIVE_FORWARDING is TRUE the forwarder MUST start a Trickle timer for that message. If the control message timer is not running and CONTROL_MESSAGE_TIMER_EXPIRATIONS is non-zero, that timer MUST be started; if it is running, it MUST be reset.

Each forwarder processes a control message to find out whether it has new data messages to receive or offer. A neighbour has a message this node lacks if the control message names a seed that is not in the Seed Set, or if the control message says the neighbour holds a sequence number above the minimum sequence number that is not in this node's Buffered Message Set. When that is the case the control message timer MUST be reset, and started if it was not running. Symmetrically, this node has a message the neighbour lacks if the control message does not mention that seed, or if the message's sequence number is at or above the neighbour's min-seqno but its bit is not set. In that case the control message timer and the timer for each such message MUST be reset, and a timer started if there was none.
sections.plainLanguage: When a data message arrives, the device checks the sequence number against the two lists and decides whether to keep it, to skip it, or to throw it away. When a control message arrives, the device compares what it holds with what the neighbour holds, and resets its retransmission timers wherever the neighbour is behind. That is how a message that was dropped in a lossy link gets sent again.

sections.title: Trickle Parameters and Their Defaults
sections.content:
PROACTIVE_FORWARDING is a boolean that says whether the forwarder schedules data message transmissions after receiving a message for the first time. Its default is TRUE, and all MPL interfaces on the same link SHOULD be configured with the same value. SEED_SET_ENTRY_LIFETIME is the minimum lifetime for an entry in the Seed Set and has a default of 30 minutes. A value that is too small can make the duplicate detection mechanism fail, so that a forwarder receives a given data message more than once.

A Trickle timer has three configuration parameters: the minimum interval size Imin, the maximum interval size Imax and a redundancy constant k. This specification adds a fourth, TimerExpirations, which gives the number of Trickle timer expiration events before the algorithm terminates for a given message. For data messages, DATA_MESSAGE_IMIN defaults to 10 times the expected link-layer latency, DATA_MESSAGE_IMAX defaults to the same value as DATA_MESSAGE_IMIN, DATA_MESSAGE_K defaults to 1 and DATA_MESSAGE_TIMER_EXPIRATIONS defaults to 3. For control messages, CONTROL_MESSAGE_IMIN defaults to 10 times the worst-case link-layer latency, CONTROL_MESSAGE_IMAX defaults to 5 minutes, CONTROL_MESSAGE_K defaults to 1 and CONTROL_MESSAGE_TIMER_EXPIRATIONS defaults to 10.

The defaults give a strategy that uses both techniques: a forwarder proactively transmits new data messages and then uses control messages to trigger additional retransmissions where drops are detected. If different nodes have different configuration parameters, Trickle may behave in unintended ways, so all interfaces attached to the same link of a given domain SHOULD use the same values.
sections.plainLanguage: The timing of the repeated sends is set by a handful of numbers: how long to wait at minimum and at most, how many copies are enough, and how many rounds to keep going. The defaults send each data message three times and keep exchanging control messages for ten rounds.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MPL uses sequence numbers to maintain a total ordering of data messages from a seed, and that can be turned into a denial-of-service attack. An attacker can spoof a message with a sufficiently large sequence number, which flushes messages from the Buffered Message Set and raises the minimum sequence number for that seed in the Seed Set. The effect is that the forwarding of data messages being disseminated is halted, and that forwarders cannot accept new messages from the seed until the sequence number rises above the new minimum or the Seed Set entry expires. The effect applies to both the proactive and the reactive modes.

More generally, the ability to inject messages into a low-power network may be used as a denial-of-service attack whatever forwarding protocol is used. Because MPL is a dissemination protocol, the ability to spoof MPL messages lets an attacker affect an entire domain. Such networks therefore rely on link-layer security to limit who can inject messages; the IEEE 802.15.4 standard specifies frame security using AES-128 for access control, message integrity, confidentiality and replay protection. If the attack vector includes attackers with access to the network, MPL SHOULD NOT be used.

To stop attackers injecting packets through a forwarder, the forwarder MUST NOT accept or forward MPL Data Messages from an interface that does not subscribe to the MPL Domain Address named in the message's destination address. Because MPL uses the Trickle algorithm to manage transmissions, the security considerations of RFC 6206 apply.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who can send fake messages can hurt MPL badly. By claiming a very high sequence number, the attacker can make every device discard the messages it is holding and refuse to accept new ones from that source. The RFC's answer is that the link layer has to keep untrusted devices off the network in the first place.

viz.caption: THE FOUR SETS A FORWARDER KEEPS

items.title: Local Interface Set
items.text: The local MPL interfaces and the unicast addresses assigned to them.

items.title: Domain Set
items.text: The MPL Domain Addresses and the local interfaces that subscribe to them.

items.title: Seed Set
items.text: One entry per seed: the seed identifier, the lowest sequence number still wanted, and the entry lifetime.

items.title: Buffered Message Set
items.text: One entry per received data message: the seed identifier, the sequence number and the message itself.

fields.name: Opt Data Len
fields.desc: Length of the option data in octets. It is variable.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Gives the length of the seed identifier: 0 means the IPv6 source address is used and the identifier is not carried.

fields.name: M
fields.desc: Set when the sequence value is known to be the largest received from that seed.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: Set to 1 in an option that does not conform to the specification. Such messages must be dropped.

fields.name: rsv
fields.desc: Reserved. Must be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.

fields.name: sequence
fields.desc: Orders the data messages from one seed. Incremented for each new message.

fields.name: seed-id
fields.desc: Identifies the seed that started the dissemination. Its length is given by the S field.
